summary: A cookbook of worked examples for JSON Object Signing and Encryption. It shows sample JSON Web Keys along with signed (JWS) and encrypted (JWE) results produced from similar inputs. Implementers can compare their output against these examples to check that their code handles keys, signing and encryption correctly. It defines no new protocol.

eli5.summary: Imagine a recipe book that shows the finished dish for each recipe. Programmers who build secret-message tools can check their own results against these pictures to see if they got it right.

subtitle: Test vectors for signing and encrypting JSON objects.

tldr.problem: Developers implementing JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) technologies need a reliable way to verify that their implementations work correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7520 provides a comprehensive set of worked examples showing JSON Web Keys (JWK), JSON Web Signatures (JWS), and JSON Web Encryption (JWE) with step-by-step input and output at each stage.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can run their code against these test vectors to check for correct handling of keys, signing and encryption. The examples are available in machine-readable format on GitHub.

today: RFC 7520 is an Informational RFC that provides test vectors for JOSE technologies. It is not superseded and remains the standard reference for validating JOSE implementations.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 7520 provides a cookbook of worked examples for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE). JOSE is a family of technologies that includes JSON Web Signature (JWS), JSON Web Encryption (JWE), JSON Web Key (JWK), and JSON Web Algorithms (JWA). These standards let applications sign and encrypt JSON data using a variety of cryptographic algorithms.

The RFC acknowledges that the full set of possible algorithm combinations is large and potentially overwhelming. Most applications use only a small subset to meet their needs. This document provides representative examples of both simple and complex JOSE operations, allowing implementers to test their code by comparing output against known good results. All examples include enough detail to be replicated, and the document notes which data are inputs versus generated during the operation.
sections.eli5: JOSE is a way to sign your name on a digital message or lock it in a digital safe. This RFC shows step-by-step examples of how to do both, so programmers can check their work.

sections.title: JSON Web Keys
sections.content:
A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON object that represents a cryptographic key. RFC 7520 provides examples of the main key types: Elliptic Curve (EC) keys, RSA keys, and symmetric keys used for both message authentication and encryption.

Each example shows the key structure with its required and optional fields. EC keys include a curve identifier (such as P-256 or P-521) and the x and y coordinates. RSA keys show the modulus, public exponent, and private exponents. Symmetric keys are simply raw byte strings encoded in base64url format. The examples emphasize important characteristics such as the required length of coordinate values and the meaning of each field.
sections.eli5: A JWK is a digital key written as JSON. The RFC shows what different kinds of keys look like: keys for elliptic curves, giant number keys for RSA, and simple secret keys.

sections.title: Signing JSON Web Signatures
sections.content:
A JSON Web Signature (JWS) cryptographically binds content to a key so recipients can verify the sender's identity and confirm the content has not been tampered with. RFC 7520 shows examples of signing using RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, RSA-PSS (probabilistic signature scheme), ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), and HMAC-SHA2 for message authentication codes.

Each example starts with input factors (the plaintext to sign, the key, and the algorithm), shows the signing operation, and displays the output in Compact Serialization, general JSON Serialization, and flattened JSON Serialization. The document also shows advanced signing scenarios: detaching the content from the signature, protecting specific header fields, and applying multiple signatures to the same content.
sections.eli5: JWS is how you digitally sign something to prove you wrote it. The RFC shows different ways to sign and what the signed message looks like.

sections.title: Encrypting JSON Web Encryption
sections.content:
JSON Web Encryption (JWE) encrypts content so only a recipient with the right key can read it. RFC 7520 illustrates encryption using several key encryption algorithms (RSA v1.5, RSA-OAEP, password-based PBES2, ECDH key agreement, and direct shared keys) paired with different content encryption algorithms (AES-HMAC-SHA2 and AES-GCM).

Each encryption example breaks down the steps: establishing input factors, generating random elements like Initialization Vectors and Content Encryption Keys, encrypting the key itself, encrypting the content, and showing the output. The examples cover practical scenarios such as compressing before encryption, including Additional Authenticated Data that is authenticated but not encrypted, and encrypting to multiple recipients simultaneously.
sections.eli5: JWE is how you lock a message so only someone with the right key can read it. The RFC shows different lock types and what the locked message looks like.

sections.title: Security Notes for Implementers
sections.content:
RFC 7520 emphasizes that the examples are designed for testing, not as production recommendations. For instance, the document does not always generate fresh random values for every example; it reuses Content Encryption Keys, Initialization Vectors, and ephemeral keys to keep the examples manageable. This simplification aids debugging but would be insecure in real deployments, where each operation must use unique random data.

The RFC points to the core JOSE specifications ([JWS], [JWE], [JWK], and [JWA]) for proper security practices. Each example notes which data are inputs versus generated, allowing readers to understand where randomness is required. Implementers using these test vectors should ensure their code generates fresh keys and random values for each actual signing or encryption operation.
sections.eli5: These examples are like practice exercises, not rules for real security. In a real program, you must use new random numbers every time, not the same ones as the examples.

viz.caption: The four main JOSE component technologies

items.title: JWK
items.text: Represents cryptographic keys as JSON objects with key type, curve, and coordinates or exponents.

items.title: JWS
items.text: Adds a digital signature to JSON content using RSA, ECDSA, HMAC or other algorithms.

items.title: JWE
items.text: Encrypts content with a symmetric key that is itself encrypted using RSA, ECDH, PBES2 or shared directly.

items.title: JWA
items.text: Specifies the cryptographic algorithms, identifiers and processing rules for JWK, JWS and JWE.
